title: Smoked Haddock and Leek Pie
subtitle: Flaked smoked haddock and leeks in a mustard cream sauce under puff pastry
excerpt: Smoked haddock and leek pie pairs the deep, saline character of smoked fish with the mildness of softened leeks in a mustard cream sauce. Puff pastry makes the lid. It is quicker to assemble than a full fish pie and has a more concentrated flavour, the smoky haddock carrying the whole dish.
sourceNotes: Smoked haddock is a cornerstone of Scottish and northern English cooking. This pie is related to the Scottish tradition of Cullen skink, a thick smoked haddock and leek soup, adapted here into a pastry-topped dish.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: Make the filling up to a day ahead and refrigerate. Top and bake on the day.

content.text: Smoked haddock and leek pie has fewer components than a full fish pie and comes together faster. The haddock poaches in milk, and that milk becomes the base of the cream sauce. The leeks cook down until completely tender before the sauce is added. Season very carefully: smoked haddock is already salty and you rarely need more than pepper.
Poach the fish and build the filling

Put the smoked haddock in a wide pan, skin side down. Pour over {{whole-milk}} of milk. Bring to a bare simmer and poach for 6 to 8 minutes until the fish flakes easily. Lift out, peel off the skin, and flake the flesh into large pieces. Reserve the poaching milk.

Wipe out the pan. Melt {{unsalted-butter}} of butter over medium heat. Add {{leek}} sliced leeks and cook for 10 minutes until fully soft. Stir in {{plain-flour}} of flour and cook for 1 minute. Gradually whisk in the warm reserved poaching milk, then {{double-cream}} of double cream. Simmer until thickened, about 5 minutes. Stir in {{dijon-mustard}} of Dijon mustard and the parsley if using. Season with pepper only, tasting before adding any salt.
Gently fold the flaked haddock into the sauce, keeping the pieces large. Transfer to the pie dish and leave to cool for 15 minutes.

Heat the oven to 200°C fan. Brush the rim of the pie dish with beaten egg. Lay the puff pastry over the filling, press down on the rim, trim, and crimp. Cut a steam vent in the centre. Brush with beaten egg. Bake for 25 to 30 minutes until the pastry is puffed and deeply golden.

items.cause: Smoked haddock releases salt into the poaching milk, which then becomes the sauce base.
items.fix: Taste the sauce before adding any salt. You almost certainly will not need any. Add pepper only.

items.symptom: The haddock has disappeared into the sauce
items.cause: The fish was broken into small pieces when folding in.
items.fix: Flake the fish into large chunks and fold gently. Large pieces hold their shape in the finished pie.

items.symptom: The sauce is thin after baking
items.cause: The filling was warm when the pastry went on.
items.fix: Let the filling cool until no steam rises before laying the pastry. The sauce continues to set as it cools.

items.symptom: The leeks are still firm inside the sauce
items.cause: They were not cooked long enough before the flour was added.
items.fix: Cook the leeks until fully tender, at least 10 minutes on medium heat, before building the sauce.

content.text: Smoked haddock is deeply embedded in British coastal food culture, particularly in Scotland, where it forms the base of Cullen skink and finnan haddie. This pie is the pastry-topped relative of those traditions, and it is one of the most flavourful and uncomplicated pies in the British repertoire. Serve with a simple green salad or buttered spinach.
